title: Paano Magtanim ng Lettuce: How to Plant Lettuce the Traditional Way

excerpt: Paano magtanim ng lettuce? Here is how traditional Filipino farmers usually plant litsugas (lettuce), step by step from getting the field ready to the harvest, with the day of each step and what to change for a higher yield.

heroImage.alt: Vegetable terraces and plastic tunnels on the slopes of Mankayan, Benguet

blocks.title: This is the traditional way
blocks.text: This guide shows how traditional farmers usually plant litsugas. Use it as a starting point. For a higher yield, update it: plant certified seed or clean planting material, test your soil, and follow the right spacing and fertilizer.

How Filipino farmers usually grow litsugas from seedlings on raised, mulched beds, the Benguet way, from sowing in a seedbed to cutting the heads or leaves about two months after transplanting. For highland growers and lowland farmers who plant it in the cool months, with the changes that give cleaner, heavier lettuce.

Before you plant, get the field ready with our [land preparation guide for vegetables](/land-preparation/vegetable-land-preparation). Then choose your seed or planting material with the [litsugas varieties sold here](/crop-varieties/lettuce). If the leaves turn pale later on, the [litsugas nutrient deficiency guide](/nutrient-deficiencies/lettuce-nutrient-deficiency) helps you find what is missing. For more on the crop, read [pagtatanim ng gulay](/crops/pagtatanim-ng-gulay), [vegetables in the Philippines](/crops/vegetables-philippines).
When to plant litsugas

In the highlands, such as La Trinidad, Atok and Buguias in Benguet, the Bukidnon uplands and the Cebu highlands, lettuce is grown all year, with rain shelters in the wettest months. In the lowlands it is grown in the cool dry months, mostly the loose leaf types, with light shade in hot weather.
What you plant
Seed, only about 150 to 200 g a hectare. Farmers soak the seed in warm water for a few hours, air dry it, and sow it thinly in seedbeds. Seedlings are pricked out once, hardened, and transplanted.
Paano magtanim ng lettuce, step by step
The crop is ready about 50 days after transplanting.
Before planting (Bago magtanim)

items.title: 14 days before transplanting: Plow and harrow twice
items.text: Plow and harrow the field two times until the soil is fine.

items.title: 3 days before transplanting: Raise and mulch the beds
items.text: Form raised beds about 1 m wide with 75 cm paths. Mix rotted chicken manure and carbonized rice hull into the bed, cover it with rice straw or plastic mulch, and punch holes 30 to 40 cm apart: two rows for head types, three rows for leaf types.

blocks.text: The nursery (Punlaan)

items.title: 36 days before transplanting: Sow in the seedbed
items.text: Make seedbeds about 1 by 10 m, mix in rotted chicken manure and carbonized rice hull, wet the bed and draw shallow lines 7 to 10 cm apart. Sow the soaked seed thinly, cover lightly and mulch with rice hull or chopped straw.

parts.title: Soak the seed, then air dry it
parts.text: Soak the seed in warm water for a few hours so it sprouts quickly and evenly. Spread it on paper or a cloth in the shade to dry a little, so the tiny seeds do not stick together in the hand.

parts.title: Ready the beds
parts.text: For one hectare of lettuce, about five seedbeds of 1 by 10 m are enough. Crush the soil fine and mix in about 1 kg of rotted chicken manure and 300 grams of carbonized rice hull for every square meter.

parts.title: Clean the soil if you can
parts.text: Some growers wet the seedbed with wood vinegar or a homemade microbe mix before sowing to keep down the fungi that kill young seedlings.

parts.title: Wet the bed and sow in lines
parts.text: Water the bed first, then draw shallow lines across it about 7 to 10 cm apart. Sprinkle the seed thinly along the lines and cover it with only a light dusting of soil.

parts.title: Mulch and water daily
parts.text: Cover the lines thinly with coir fiber, fine rice hull or straw chopped short to keep the top moist, and water every day with a fine sprinkler can.

items.title: 21 days before transplanting: Prick out the seedlings
items.text: At the two leaf stage, about two weeks after sowing, move the seedlings to another bed or to trays so each has room. Give light shade in hot weather and a plastic roof in the rains.

parts.title: Wait for two leaves
parts.text: Prick the seedlings when they show their first two leaves, about two weeks after sowing.

parts.title: Fill the trays
parts.text: Fill nursery trays or another bed with a loose mix that has vermicompost in it. The rich, soft mix helps the moved seedlings recover quickly.

parts.title: Move one seedling a cell
parts.text: Lift the seedlings with a little soil on the roots, holding them by a leaf, and set one in each tray cell. Firm the mix around it and water gently.

parts.title: Shade in the dry months, roof in the rains
parts.text: Keep the trays under light shade in the hot season and under a plastic roof in the rainy season, and water every day. They go to the field about three weeks after pricking.

items.title: 7 days before transplanting: Harden the seedlings
items.text: In the last week, water less often and give the seedlings full sun so they do not wilt after transplanting.

blocks.text: Planting day (Pagtatanim)

items.title: Transplanting day: Transplant in the afternoon
items.text: Water the holes, put a little complete fertilizer (14 14 14) in each, then set one seedling a hole and press the soil around it. Replace any that die right away.

blocks.text: Care while it grows (Pag aalaga)

items.title: Day 1: Keep the beds moist
items.text: Water regularly, enough to keep the soil damp but never soggy.

items.title: Day 15: First side dressing
items.text: Give each plant a small pinch of urea, mixed half and half with muriate of potash (0 0 60) for head lettuce. Leaf lettuce needs only this one urea feeding.

items.title: Day 20: Scout for loopers and rot
items.text: Look for green loopers and aphids under the leaves and for soft, slimy rot at the base. Remove rotting plants.

items.title: Day 30: Second side dressing for head lettuce
items.text: Head lettuce gets a second small feeding of urea and potash about a month after transplanting.

items.title: Day 50: Sort and pack cool
items.text: Sort in the field, pack in boxes with holes, and keep them cool and shaded until they reach the buyer.

blocks.text: Harvest (Anihan)

items.title: Day 50: Harvest early in the morning
items.text: Cut leaf lettuce when it reaches market size and before it bolts. Head lettuce is cut when the heads are firm, about 45 to 60 days after transplanting. Harvest early so the leaves do not wilt.

blocks.text: Spacing, water and fertilizer for litsugas
Spacing
Raised beds about 1 m wide with 75 cm paths. Holes 30 to 40 cm apart, two rows a bed for head types and three rows for leaf types. One seedling a hole.
Water
Seedbeds are watered daily. The field by sprinkler, hose or furrow, keeping the soil evenly moist. Mulch keeps the leaves clean and the soil from drying or splashing. Standing water brings rot.
Fertilizer

Beds get rotted chicken manure, about 1 kg a square meter, and carbonized rice hull before transplanting. At transplanting a little 14 14 14 goes in each hole, then urea, with potash for head lettuce, at about 15 and 30 days. Many highland growers also water with manure tea or fermented plant juice. To read what a bag really gives, see our guide to [fertilizer for this crop](/blog/fertilizer-for-vegetables-philippines).
Care and harvest
Care while it grows
Pricking and hardening of seedlings, raised beds under straw or plastic mulch, regular watering, one or two small side dressings, and close watch for loopers, aphids and rot.
When and how to harvest

Leaf lettuce is cut from about a month after transplanting, before it bolts. Head lettuce at about 45 to 60 days, when the heads are firm. Farmers cut early in the morning, sort in the field and pack in boxes with holes, kept cool on the way to market.
Common mistakes when planting litsugas

items: Transplanting soft seedlings that were never hardened, so many wilt.
Planting head types in the hot lowland months, so they bolt and turn bitter.
Leaving the beds bare, so rain splashes soil on the leaves and rot sets in.
Too much urea late in the crop, which gives soft, quick rotting leaves.
Harvesting at midday or packing in closed sacks.

blocks.text: How to get a higher yield of litsugas
The traditional way gets a crop, but small changes add up. These are the first things to change, one season at a time.

items: Choose varieties for your elevation and season, with heat tolerant leaf types for the lowlands.
Test the soil and feed by the result, with compost or rotted manure plus small, timed side dressings.
Raise seedlings under a rain shelter and harden them a week before transplanting.
Use raised, mulched beds and sun the prepared beds for a week to reduce rot.
Scout weekly and keep the plants cool from harvest to market.

items.q: How far apart do you plant litsugas?
items.a: Raised beds about 1 m wide with 75 cm paths. Holes 30 to 40 cm apart, two rows a bed for head types and three rows for leaf types.

items.q: How long before litsugas can be harvested?
items.a: It is ready about 50 days after transplanting. Leaf lettuce is cut from about a month after transplanting, before it bolts.
